excerpts.text: SHA-256 stands for Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit.

The “256” is the size of its output: every input, whether a single character or a multi-gigabyte disk image, produces a digest of exactly 256 bits. That is 32 bytes, usually written as 64 hexadecimal characters.

excerpts.text: It produces a 256-bit (32-byte) digest from 512-bit input blocks, using an 8-word internal state and a 64-round compression function – roughly double the state size of SHA-1 with 16 fewer rounds per block.

Bitcoin’s proof-of-work mining and block hashing both run on SHA-256. Every public TLS certificate issued since 2016 is signed with it (or something stronger). Windows code signing, package managers, and most Git tooling built after 2020 default to it as well. NIST’s current guidance puts SHA-256’s collision resistance at roughly 2^128 operations (the generic birthday bound for a 256-bit output, which is not the same as unconditional 2^128 security against every possible attack) and its preimage resistance at 2^256 – numbers that remain firmly in “not happening with today’s compute” territory.
